title: Python async (asyncio), Part 7: locks, events, context and threads
tldr: One thread is not one-at-a-time: any await between reading shared state and writing it is a gap where other Tasks run. Measured on the gateway: a call counter read, awaited and written by 10 Tasks ends at 1; a cache that checks, awaits seller-c and stores asks it 100 times for 100 requests; and a log tag kept in a module variable stamps shopper-2's id on shopper-1's line. Then the tools, each traced to CPython 3.14's locks.py: Lock (fair, not owned by a Task), Event, Condition, Semaphore and BoundedSemaphore again, and Barrier (3.11+); and contextvars, where every Task runs in a copy of the context current when it was created. Gateway v8 adds a single-flight price cache (100 requests for one item make one call to each seller, and seller-e's 900 ms price is cached for the requests that come after), a request id that follows the work into Tasks, logs and seller-e's SDK thread, and the three thread bridges: to_thread or run_in_executor with copy_context().run, call_soon_threadsafe and run_coroutine_threadsafe; plus what the free-threaded 3.14 build changes. Then what breaks: a lock held across a 900 ms call, a deadlock from lock order, context lost or wrong in thread pools and callbacks (different on the free-threaded build), loop objects touched from the wrong thread or loop, and cache herds at 10 times the load. Ends with lock vs single-flight vs an owner Task vs an immutable snapshot, and an interview drill.
